I mean, the night was difficult, it was a five and a half hour town hall. But the loudest voices were the ugliest, and people were unkind and unfair, and some of them have continued to be. I don't think politics has to be that way and I don't think it should be that way. I didn't agree in many respects with our last president. And people forget it was losing my daughter. I had insurance, but we still had over a million dollars in medical bills. And that was difficult in addition to the heartache of losing a child that I loved very much to have that burden too, I think really does make me understand the issue. I also saw my dad struggle with my mother's medical bill. She died when I was four. He had no insurance and she had had cancer for four years. He was paying off medical bills for decades. turn_text: Can you go into more detail specifically about the amendment?

It was really quite simple. It gave the states more flexibility to not slavishly follow federal mandates. That was the balance. that it allowed people to remain insured. It kept the federal government involved in helping, but it simply gave the states more flexibility. So states could allow insurers to offer different kinds of insurance policies other than the federally mandated ones. States could create high-risk pools And they were encouraged to, in fact, to help those who were at risk of losing insurance. States could raise rates differently than the federal government prescribed, but only if they created those high-risk bulls. And then we created a fund, a large fund, to help them actually create those funds. That was the balance. Where do we get the federal government to help? And where do we get the federal government to have a little bit of a lighter touch on this issue? And it was enough to get the conservatives on board without losing the moderates.
So from that town hall and from that amendment, you navigated some muddy waters to say the least. What was the biggest lesson from that process?

I think for me personally, it certainly showed me the importance of the ability to compromise. I think it's been a hallmark of my time in Congress. I really try very hard to not just find common ground with other people, but also compromise with other people. You don't have common ground. And will you swallow something you don't like in order to get something that you need? And you let the other person also have the same victory where they get something they need. It certainly validated that. I think for me, I also came to realize that we're in a very tense political environment, and there are people who hate the president, and I discovered that night and since they not only hate the president, they hate anyone who doesn't hate the president. And so that's become like the new litmus test, that nothing else I say will matter to some people because I don't sufficiently hate the president in their mind. That's unfortunate. I don't like that's good for politics in America.

turn_text: So an issue that is affecting every community, every state, probably internationally is the heroin epidemic. Well, it's an issue I'm very involved in. I chair the heroin task force, bipartisan task force in Congress. And there's no part of society that's unaffected by this. And unlike prior drug epidemics, this heroin crisis is most frequently starting in people's medicine chest, not on the streets. People are getting addicted to opioids legally. And then feeding that dependency illegally and moving from, you know, legally prescribed pills to heroin on the streets because it's the only thing they can get. It's a desperate, desperate crisis and we're sitting in an area in Ocean County that was recently named a Haida high intensity drug trafficking area. And we're getting some more DEA resource here for that, excuse me, for that reason. So it's devastating. I don't think anyone doesn't know somebody. I mean, I have friends. I have a very, very close friend of mine who died of addiction. I have friends who've lost children. And it's just devastating. And I think there are things that we can do at every level. I think most of the treatment really has to happen locally. because it's got to be person to person. I think the federal government can help support that. We can help with the best practices. I think there are things at the federal level that can and must be supported like funding things like high intensity drug trafficking areas so we can bring resource. I think changing the way prescriptions are given. There's a bell that I've co-sponsored that would put a federal limit of 10 days on opioids. States can do shorter if they want. But if there's no state limit, there's a 10 day federal limit. There's things we can do about funding. For example, right now there's a rule in Medicare that limits Medicaid, I'm sorry, that limits the institutions that can be reimbursed by Medicaid to those with 16 beds or fewer. If somebody's desperately needing to be in a treatment center, it doesn't really matter if there are 16 beds or 17 beds. And it's this artificial limit that causes Medicaid to not reimburse a lot of institutions, I think, as a problem. We have a bell working on fixing that.
